newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA'S AFBRAND PLANS DEBT CUTS, ACQUISITIONS.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA'S AFBRAND PLANS DEBT CUTS, ACQUISITIONS.

text.p: Afribrand Holdings Ltd, a South African confectionary and snacks group which is to list on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange on August 5, said it would apply nearly half of its 35 million rand listing capital to cut debt.

The group which supplies branded sweets and snacks to wholesalers and the informal sector, said on Tuesday 16 million rand would be used to smoothe debt, six million would go to capital spending and the rest to expansion and acquisitions.

"Within the businesses themselves we will be looking to pay off debt as a start. We also have a certain amount of equipment arriving from across the water in the next few weeks, getting us ready for Christmas," chief executive Stephen Weir said.
"And then we will have some funds available for acquisitions and future expansion and the introduction of new lines," he told a pre-listing presentation.

In choosing acquisitions, the group would continue to focus on its core operations of supplying food products to the lower income market, but it would also consider other informal sector opportunities.
"Anything that ends up on a hawker's (street vendor's) table, will have some interest to us," Weir said.

The group, which is to list in the food sector under the abbreviated name Afbrand, has forecast a 41 percent surge in earnings per share to 9.4 cents for the year to end-May 1998 and a dividend of 2.4 cents. An earnings jump of 26 percent and a dividend of 3.0 cents is predicted for 1999.

Weir said Afbrand was firmly entrenched in major growth markets. Wholesalers were growing at around 25 percent per annum, the lower income end of the market by 40 percent a year and the salted snacks market by between 25 and 30 percent.
Exports into the rest of Africa were also taking off, with markets in Senegal, Angola, Zaire, Angola and Zambia already being tested.

Afbrand's share offer comprises a 22.0 million rand private placing, which Weir said had been eagerly snapped up by institutions, a 3.0 million rand preferential offer -- which he said was 40 times subscribed -- and a 10 million rand public offer.

Shareholding would see management retain a 55 percent chunk, insitutions and asset managers 18 percent, the group's merchant bank Standard Corporate and Merchant Bank five percent, Western Cape-based group Brimstone nine percent and the public 13 percent.
